title: People usually leave a short quiet between turns, in many languages
summary: In a ten-language study, people answering yes-or-no questions usually avoided talking over each other and kept the quiet between turns short.
body: Stivers, Enfield, and colleagues videoed informal conversation in ten languages on five continents and timed the move from a yes-or-no question to its answer. Every language showed the same broad shape: people generally avoided overlap, and they kept the silence between turns short. The most common timing in each language was a tiny gap, not a long pause. Average waits still differed by language, so the shared shape is not a claim that every community pauses for one identical length. The authors treat question-and-answer pairs as a window on turn-taking, not as a recording of every kind of talk.

sources.title: Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation
sources.author: Tanya Stivers, N. J. Enfield, and colleagues
sources.note: Supports the ten-language finding of avoidance of overlap and minimization of silence, with modes between a zero gap and a short positive gap, and quantitative differences in averages. Peer-reviewed open copy.
